correctness.rationale: The extension lemma is valid with overlapping border occurrences allowed. A suffix border of the extended word of length at most b, where b is the old longest-border length, would also occur at the start of the second copy of the old longest border, giving a third occurrence. Any longer new border, with its last letter deleted, would be an old border, so only length b+1 can witness closedness. Matching the context letter extends both old copies without creating a third. Reversal gives the left test. In the proposed word the interior block occupies positions a+2 through a+8. The two long zero blocks flank it; for the indexed row their clipped portions both have length a+2−j≥2 and the interior zeros are singletons, giving exactly two border occurrences. The other proposed borders each occur exactly twice by the displayed run positions; in particular the long 1-zero border selects the first and last long zero runs, whose lengths are at least two even in the exceptional case. In all rows the available context letters differ on each compared side. The endpoints straddle the prescribed cut and are distinct. The indexed row contributes a−2, including zero for (2,1), and seven fixed intervals give a+5=floor(n/2)+1. The parameters cover every n≥13; the proof neither needs nor establishes an upper bound on F₂(n).
residual_risks: The finite output only tests the witness and a finite subset of cut enumerations; the proof is the evidence for the infinite bound.

evidence: Proposition 14 places the cut before the unique b in a^m b a^m or a^m b a^{m+1}, with m=floor((n−1)/2) nested occurrences. The general crossing upper bound 3(n−1) does not give a stronger lower bound. General enumeration work concerns the occurrences of a supplied word.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These results do not yield the larger lower bound on either parity; the odd/even gains over that lower construction are one/two. This is not a comparison against a proved extremal optimum.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The exact seed and knowledge that a witness exists at n=14 do not imply that elongating the two zero runs preserves the old maximal occurrences and supplies additional ones. Both require checking for lost maximality or a third border occurrence; the parameterized context proof does this, and handles odd lengths including n=13.

evidence: The sources count positional occurrences, not word types, and the maximality condition is no closed one-character extension on either available side. The run-length paper represents the same occurrences by valid pairs and longest borders.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: One-based versus zero-based indexing and omission of irrelevant singleton cases do not change the comparison. The known valid-pair framework makes the proof natural but does not supply its all-length family.

value.rationale: The additive improvement matters here because the inequality crosses the exact half benchmark at every n≥13 and even the rounded-up benchmark at every even length from 14. The result explains how the same fixed run pattern maintains the phenomenon as the length grows, rather than merely giving another isolated optimum or extrapolating a census. It provides a reusable explicit test family for cut-query analyses. It does not claim a better asymptotic density coefficient or refute a published conjecture.
residual_risks: The true extremal growth rate and exact larger-length maxima remain outside the finding.
